extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions' administrators, Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and applying the final Title IX definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment, including how to balance that definition with First Amendment, academic freedom, religious liberty, and freedom of association concerns. Covers factors to evaluate harassment, limits on regulatory reach, and recipient obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hostile environment sex-based harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition in the final regulations covers only sex-based conduct that is unwelcome, both subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retains the 2020 amendments' reference to offensiveness; the definition is intended to be narrowly tailored to advance the compelling government interest in eliminating sex discrimination. The definition requires an actual effect (limiting or denying participation/benefit) rather than merely a 'purpose' to interfere. The regulations prohibit only conduct that meets all these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements must all be satisfied (not open-ended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations only prohibit conduct that meets all the elements—that the conduct is unwelcome, sex-based, subjectively and objectively offensive, and so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies a person's ability to participate in or benefit from the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition is not an open-ended discretionary inquiry; it requires each listed element. The reference to the 'totality of the circumstances' is meant to ensure context is considered and that no required element or relevant factual consideration is ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of circumstances factors for evaluating hostile environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations enumerate long-established factors relevant to determining whether conduct created a hostile environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include: the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the education program or activity; the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; the parties' ages, roles within the program or activity, previous interactions, and other relevant characteristics of each party; the location of the conduct and the context in which it occurred; and other established instances of sex-based harassment in the recipient's program or activity. These factors are intended to ensure context-sensitive assessments and to avoid inappropriately sweeping in conduct or speech that does not actually create a hostile environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow tailoring and First Amendment compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The final definition is narrowly tailored and, as written, does not infringe constitutional First Amendment rights because it targets conduct that has the actual effect of limiting or denying participation or benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department distinguishes this definition from policies struck down or enjoined in cases like Saxe and Speech First by emphasizing clarity, narrow scope, and the requirement of actual effect and objective and subjective offensiveness. The definition does not single out particular viewpoints and applies regardless of the view expressed. Courts' doctrines (e.g., Tinker, Harris) support narrowly drawn anti-harassment rules. Nonetheless, the First Amendment may constrain the manner of a recipient's response (for example, favoring remedies other than discipline in some circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.6(d) — protection of First Amendment rights in application
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.6(d) continues to state that nothing in the Title IX regulations requires a recipient to restrict any rights that would otherwise be protected from government action by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must formulate, interpret, and apply rules in a manner that respects legal rights of students and employees. Recipients remain free to determine whether discipline is an appropriate response to sex-based harassment and, if so, what form that discipline should take. The Department will offer technical assistance to promote compliance and appropriate application of the definition so as not to infringe First Amendment rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic freedom and academic-context considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the Title IX regulations restricts the academic freedom of faculty or requires or prohibits particular curricular materials; the academic setting of conduct is highly relevant to the harassment determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that might amount to harassment in other settings may not do so within appropriate academic discourse, especially in postsecondary academic contexts. The regulation governing curricular materials (§106.42) remains unchanged. Given the fact-based nature of hostile-environment determinations and the relevance of academic context, the Department did not find it necessary to revise §106.6(d) to explicitly protect academic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious liberty and freedom of association considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX regulations do not require recipients to restrict free exercise of religion or freedom of association; institutions controlled by a religious organization are not subject to Title IX to the extent application would be inconsistent with religious tenets (20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(3) and §106.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should not be required or encouraged by the regulations to punish religious exercise or speech. Student groups may impose membership criteria not related to sex that promote the group's mission (for example, requiring a legitimate good faith interest in the mission). The Department notes other enforcement avenues (e.g., DOJ enforcement of Title IV) for religious discrimination claims in public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to private recipients and state-law preemption issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.6(d) applies to all recipients of Federal financial assistance, including private recipients; nothing in the final regulations requires a private recipient to restrict rights otherwise protected by the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR interprets Title IX consistently with First Amendment principles and will not interpret the regulations to lead to suppression of protected speech. Title IX and the final regulations do not preempt State laws that govern speech protected by the First Amendment as applied to private recipients; however, a recipient's obligation to comply with Title IX is not obviated by a conflicting State law governing speech that is not protected by the First Amendment. See the discussion of §106.6(b) for preemption considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement approach, non-prejudgment, and technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will enforce the Title IX regulations through its complaint process, will provide technical assistance, and will not prejudge whether specific cases comply with Title IX prior to fact-specific investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will address improper implementation through complaints and assistance but cannot comment on identified situations or hypotheticals without conducting investigations. The Department does not anticipate enforcing the regulations in a way that would require recipients to adopt constitutionally impermissible restrictions, and it emphasizes recipients have ample means other than disciplinary action to remedy hostile environments.
